title: A Lethal Mutation of Servant Leadership
author: Regenerative Schools
summary: If you're reading this as an educator, I'm interested in your experience of last school year. I'm interested in what the poll will find as normal, since in my experience, these kinds of burnout behaviors are ubiquitous among educators. In fact, despite spending the past nine months writing a book and a substack about burnout, I am still constantly reminding myself not to fall back into these same unhealthy mindsets and habits. I've been wondering lately if the self-erasure that I'm prone to is the dark side of the servant leadership that I've heard about my whole life. It's an uncomfortable question to ponder. The basic definition of servant leadership is that leaders should put others first instead of leading with ego, treat everyone with respect regardless of their rank, and lift up others' needs instead of leading from a desire for prestige or power. Research shows that organizations that adopt servant leadership have "stronger employee engagement, better retention, and a culture of trust." Those findings track with my own experience: when I think of the most effective leaders I ever worked with, they were profoundly humble and tuned in to others' needs. We need many more servant leaders like them in our schools and in our world. All of this points to servant leadership as an unalloyed good for schools. I'd much rather work for a selfless leader than a selfish one any day. So why am I wondering if this clearly positive concept has played a role in my own burnout? To understand my uncomfortable question, it helps to understand another concept in education: the lethal mutation. William Jones defines lethal mutation as "an idea or a practice that is prompted by sound scientific evidence, but is implemented in a way that reduces, or even completely negates, its effectiveness." I worry that servant leadership suffers from a lethal mutation: too often, being humble and other-centered can mutate into self-erasure. Consider the following statistics: In one survey, school leaders reported worse well-being than almost any other working adult, with 85% reporting serious daily stress. In another, more than half of school leaders report that their stress levels are so high they are considering a career change or retirement. Half of all new principals leave the principalship within their first three years of service. Just as our profession is facing a profound crisis of teacher burnout and attrition, we're also facing the same dual crises in our school leaders. Now, I'm not saying that the primary cause of the educator burnout crisis is this mindset. The research on burnout is clear: it's caused by structural mismatches between employees and their work places. However, I do wonder if the servant leadership mindset can exacerbate this crisis. Servants, by definition, can't really say no to requests. Can't set boundaries. When your identity as a leader is "the one who serves," where is the space for your own needs? Self-erasure is not sustainable for very long. There's a gendered element to this lethal mutation as well. Women spend their whole lives encouraged to put others' needs first. So we women leaders often naturally tend toward this mindset, leaning into being indispensable, feeling the need to prove our worth as leaders. For us women, the concept of "servant leadership" can be just another nudge towards burnout, among many other nudges. The research bears out my experience. Women for years have reported higher rates of burnout than men, leading experts to coin the term "the burnout gap." Women are also less likely to share their levels of fatigue, causing their exhaustion to be underestimated by others. The shadow side of servant leadership is particularly dark for women. The Way Forward So if we eschew ego-driven leadership because it hurts others, and we eschew the lethal mutation of servant leadership because it hurts ourselves, what is the path forward? How can we retain what's beneficial from this mindset, while leaving behind what is harmful? Regenerative farms can show us a way forward, with the ethos of mutual flourishing . Regenerative farms ensure that their soil is healthy. They rotate years of crops and fallow years- pasture cover that rejuvenates the soil- because they know that depleted soil can't grow thriving crops. In the same way, regenerative leaders know that modeling unchecked service is ultimately harmful to the school culture. When we're chronically stressed, we lose empathy and flexible thinking, the very things we need to do our jobs well. Also, when we model depletion for teachers, they'll be more likely to deplete themselves. And if we all model depletion for students, they'll grow up to be just as stressed and exhausted as we are. Is this really what we want for our children? You might not be able to change all of the structural causes of burnout, but you can model a regenerative mindset. Sustainable habits take courage: admitting your limits, setting boundaries on your workday, choosing not to push past your capacity. So go back to your answer to the poll at the beginning of this essay. Which of these behaviors do you want to change? What is your next right step in embodying mutual flourishing instead of depletion? Caring for yourself is not at odds with caring for others. When you lead from a place of groundedness instead of from a place of overwhelm, your well-being impacts everyone around you. This is the vision for regenerative leadership: not ego and power, not servitude and self-erasure, but mutual thriving.
